items.prompt: Which of these is a gas?

options.why: Water in a glass is a liquid.
An ice cube is a solid.
A wooden block is a solid.

hints: Gases are often invisible.
A gas spreads out to fill its container.
What fills up a balloon when you blow into it?
items.explanation: Air is a mixture of gases. It spreads out to fill the whole balloon.

items.prompt: Sort the materials into solids, liquids and gases.
hints: Solids keep their shape.
Liquids flow and take the shape of their container.
Be careful with sand: look at one grain.
items.explanation: Stone, ice and sand are solids, and each grain of sand keeps its shape. Milk, oil and honey are liquids, and air, water vapour and helium are gases.

items.prompt: Match each state to its property.
pairs: flows and takes the shape of its container
spreads out to fill all the space it is in
hints: Think about an ice cube, water and air.
Which one stays the same shape on a table?
Which one escapes from an open bottle?
items.explanation: A solid keeps its shape and a liquid flows to take the shape of its container. A gas spreads out to fill all the space.

items.prompt: Sand can be poured like a liquid. Why is sand still a solid?

options.text: Each grain keeps its own shape and size.

options.why: Dry sand pours too, and it is still a solid.
Being heavy does not make something a solid.
Sand sinks. Floating does not decide the state anyway.

hints: Look closely at a single grain.
Does one grain change shape when you pour it?
Think about the properties of a solid.
items.explanation: Sand is made of tiny solid grains. Each grain keeps its shape, even though the grains can be poured.

items.prompt: Ani pours 200 ml of juice from a tall glass into a wide bowl. How much juice is in the bowl?

options.text: less than 200 ml, because it spreads out
options.why: The juice looks lower, but none of it has gone.

options.text: more than 200 ml, because the bowl is bigger
options.why: A bigger bowl does not make more juice.

options.text: none, because juice turns into a gas
options.why: The juice stays a liquid when it is poured.

hints: Liquids change shape when they are poured.
Was any juice spilled or added?
Does the amount change, or only the shape?
items.explanation: A liquid takes the shape of its container, but its volume stays the same. The bowl holds the same 200 ml.

items.prompt: Choose 2 properties of gases.

options.text: They spread out to fill their container.

options.why: Solids keep a fixed shape. Gases do not.

options.text: They can be squashed into a smaller space.

options.why: Most gases, like air, have no colour.
Gases move and spread out all the time.

hints: Think about air in a bicycle pump.
Think about a smell spreading across a room.
Cross out properties of solids.
items.explanation: Gases spread out to fill any container. They can also be squashed, which is how a bicycle pump works.

items.prompt: Two syringes are sealed at the tip. One holds air and one holds water. Which plunger can you push in further?

options.text: the one with water, because water is runny
options.why: Liquids flow, but they are very hard to squash.

options.text: the one with air, because gases can be squashed
both the same, because they are the same size
options.why: Air and water behave differently when squashed.
The air can be squashed, so its plunger moves in.

hints: Both syringes are sealed, so nothing can escape.
Which state can be squashed into a smaller space?
Think about pumping air into a ball.
items.explanation: Gases can be squashed, so the air plunger moves in. Liquids hardly squash at all, so the water plunger barely moves.

items.prompt: Which of these is a liquid?

options.why: Salt is made of tiny solid crystals.
A stone is a solid.
A wooden spoon is a solid.

hints: Liquids flow and can be poured.
Liquids take the shape of their container.
Which one could you pour as a runny stream?
items.explanation: Cooking oil flows and takes the shape of its container, so it is a liquid. Salt pours too, but each crystal is solid.

items.prompt: Water as a gas is called water ___.
hints: It forms when water evaporates.
It is invisible in the air.
The word starts with v.
items.explanation: Water as a gas is called water vapour. It is invisible and mixes with the air.

items.prompt: Someone is cooking fried rice in the kitchen. Soon you can smell it in the bedroom. Why?

options.text: Smells are solids that roll along the floor.
options.why: Smells are not solid. They travel through the air.

options.text: Smells are liquids that flow under doors.
options.why: Smells are not liquid. They travel as a gas.
Smells are real. A gas carries them to your nose.

options.text: The smell is carried by a gas that spreads through the air.

hints: Smells reach your nose through the air.
Which state spreads out to fill a space?
Think about how the smell got so far.
items.explanation: Gases spread out to fill the space they are in. The gas carrying the smell spreads through the house to your nose.

items.prompt: A sealed bottle holds 1 litre of air. Another holds 1 litre of water. Which statement is true?

options.text: The water has much more mass, but the air still has some mass.
The air has no mass at all.
options.why: Air does have mass. A litre of air has a mass of about 1 gram.

options.text: They have the same mass, because the volumes are the same.
options.why: Same volume does not mean same mass. Water has much more.

options.text: The air could be poured into a cup like the water.
options.why: Air spreads out. It cannot be poured into a cup like water.

hints: Air is a real material.
You can feel air push on you when the wind blows.
A litre of water has a mass of 1 kilogram.
items.explanation: A litre of water has a mass of about 1 kg, while a litre of air has a mass of about 1 g. Air is light, but it still has mass.

items.prompt: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?

options.why: A liquid takes the shape of its container.
A gas spreads out to fill its container.
Water vapour is a gas, so it spreads out.

hints: Think about a stone in a bowl.
The shape does not change when you move it.
A liquid and a gas both change shape.
items.explanation: A solid keeps its own shape wherever you put it.

items.prompt: Tap the liquid.

figure.alt: Three kitchen things: bread on the left, a carton of milk in the middle and a cookie on the right.

hints: A liquid flows and can be poured.
You drink it from a carton.
Bread and cookies are solids.
items.explanation: Milk flows and can be poured, so it is a liquid. Bread and a cookie are solids.

items.prompt: Label what is inside the closed bottle. Air is a gas you cannot see.

figure.alt: A closed bottle with a red cap. The bottom half is full of blue water with a grey stone resting at the bottom. The top half looks empty.

hints: The stone is hard and keeps its shape.
The water flows and fills the bottom.
The top part is not empty. Air fills it.
items.explanation: The stone is a solid, the water is a liquid and the air in the top is a gas.

items.prompt: Complete the table. Use the words solid, liquid, gas, yes or no.
items.caption: Squashing materials
head: Material
State
Easy to squash?
hints: A gas can be squashed into a smaller space.
Milk is a liquid and is hard to squash.
Air is a gas.
items.explanation: Wood and milk are hard to squash. Air is a gas and is easy to squash.

items.prompt: Look at the syringe results. What do they show?

head: Syringe holds
Start (ml)
After pushing (ml)
figure.alt: Table of two sealed syringes. Air started at 10 ml and was pushed to 4 ml. Water started at 10 ml and stayed at 10 ml.

options.text: Water can be squashed more than air
options.why: The water stayed at 10 ml, so it was not squashed.

options.text: Air and water squash by the same amount
options.why: The air went from 10 ml to 4 ml and the water stayed at 10 ml.

options.text: Air can be squashed into a smaller space but water cannot
Neither air nor water can be squashed
options.why: The air was squashed from 10 ml to 4 ml.

hints: Compare the start and end for each syringe.
Which volume got smaller?
Think about which state can be squashed.
items.explanation: The air was pushed into a smaller space. The water volume did not change, so a liquid is hard to squash.

items.prompt: A jug holds 750 ml of juice. Dewi pours 3 cups of 150 ml each. How much juice is left?
hints: Find how much juice is poured out altogether.
Multiply 3 by 150.
Take that amount away from 750.
items.explanation: 3 x 150 = 450 ml is poured out. 750 - 450 = 300 ml is left.

items.prompt: Sort each material into the correct state.
hints: Sugar grains and a sponge both keep their own shape.
Honey and ink flow.
Oxygen and helium spread out in the air.
items.explanation: Sugar and a sponge are solids, honey and ink are liquids, and oxygen and helium are gases.

items.prompt: Dewi squashes a sponge and it changes shape. She says it is not a solid. What is the best reply?

options.text: She is right, a sponge is a liquid
options.why: A sponge does not flow or take the shape of a container.

options.text: It is a solid with air holes, and it springs back to its shape
She is right, a sponge is a gas
options.why: A sponge does not spread out to fill a space.

options.text: A sponge is not a material
options.why: A sponge is made of a material and it is a solid object.

hints: A liquid flows. Does a sponge flow?
A sponge returns to its shape after being squeezed.
Think about the tiny holes full of air.
items.explanation: A sponge keeps its shape and goes back to it when you let go. The air in its holes squashes, but the sponge is a solid.

items.prompt: Match each state to an example in the kitchen.
hints: A spoon keeps its shape.
Cooking oil can be poured.
A balloon is filled with air.
items.explanation: A wooden spoon is a solid, cooking oil is a liquid and air in a balloon is a gas.

items.prompt: Choose 2 properties of liquids.

options.why: Only a solid keeps its own shape.

options.text: takes the shape of its container
is easy to squash into a smaller space
options.why: That is a property of a gas.

hints: Think about pouring juice into a glass.
The juice changes shape but stays the same amount.
Choose the two properties that fit pouring.
items.explanation: A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.

items.prompt: A sealed syringe holds 10 ml of air. Maya pushes the plunger until it reads 5 ml. What has happened to the air?

options.text: Half of the air has disappeared
options.why: The syringe is sealed, so no air can escape.

options.text: The air has turned into a liquid
options.why: Squashing does not change air into a liquid here.

options.text: The air has turned into a solid
options.why: Squashing air does not make it solid.

options.text: The same air is squashed into a smaller space

hints: The syringe is sealed.
Air cannot get in or out.
Think about what changes: the amount of air or the space it takes up.
items.explanation: No air escaped because the syringe is sealed. The air is squashed so it takes up less space.

items.prompt: A material that flows and takes the shape of its container is a ___.
hints: Think about water in a cup.
It is not a solid or a gas.
The word starts with the letter l.
items.explanation: A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.

items.prompt: A solid keeps its own ___. A gas spreads out to fill all the ___ it can.
hints: Think about a stone and a balloon.
A stone does not change its form.
A gas fills the whole container.
items.explanation: A solid keeps its shape. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can.

items.prompt: Put these in order, from hardest to squash to easiest to squash.
hints: A gas is the easiest to squash.
A solid is the hardest to squash.
A liquid is in the middle.
items.explanation: A brick is a solid and is very hard to squash. Water is hard to squash. Air is easy to squash.

items.prompt: A football has a mass of 410 g. After it is pumped with air, its mass is 425 g. What does this show?

options.why: The football got heavier, so the air must have mass.
The football got heavier, not lighter.
A ball cannot add mass on its own. The mass came from the air.

hints: Compare the two masses.
What was added to the ball?
Subtract 410 from 425.
items.explanation: The extra 15 g comes from the air pumped in, so air has mass.

items.prompt: The chart shows the mass of 100 ml of each liquid. Which liquid has the most mass?

figure.alt: Bar chart of the mass of 100 ml of each liquid. Honey 142 g, oil 92 g, water 100 g, milk 103 g.

options.why: Water is 100 g, which is less than honey.
Oil is the lightest here at 92 g.
Milk is 103 g, which is less than honey.

hints: Look for the tallest bar.
The volume is the same for each liquid.
The tallest bar has the most mass.
items.explanation: Honey has the tallest bar, 142 g for 100 ml. Different liquids can have different masses for the same volume.
